story_description: Implement the central coordination layer that orchestrates registry fetching, caching, and installation, exposing a unified ObservableObject API for SwiftUI consumption in onboarding and settings screens.
task_description: Create the main orchestrator class that combines RegistryFetcher, RegistryCache, and RegistryInstaller into a cohesive facade, managing async refresh flows, error handling, and published state for UI binding.
atom_description: Implement RegistryCoordinator as an ObservableObject in Blaze/Sources/Registry/RegistryCoordinator.swift that serves as the single entry point for all registry operations. The coordinator exposes @Published properties for skills, plugins, and agents arrays, loading state, error state, and installation progress. It orchestrates the fetch-cache-install pipeline by delegating to RegistryFetcher for network requests, RegistryCache for SQLite persistence with 24h TTL, and RegistryInstaller for file system operations. The coordinator handles automatic cache refresh on launch, manual refresh triggers, background refresh scheduling, and graceful degradation when offline. It provides async methods for loadRegistry(), refreshRegistry(force:), installItem(_:), uninstallItem(_:), and checkForUpdates(). Error handling includes retry logic with exponential backoff, offline mode detection, and user-friendly error message generation.
problem_statement: The Blaze app has separate components for fetching (R002), caching (R003), and installing (R004) registry items, but no unified API to orchestrate these operations. Without a coordinator, UI code would need to manually sequence fetch-cache-install operations, handle errors at multiple levels, and manage complex async state. The coordinator provides a clean ObservableObject facade that encapsulates all registry complexity and exposes simple published properties for SwiftUI binding.

edge_cases: Network request times out during loadRegistry() - should retry then fall back to cache
Cache is corrupted or unreadable - should clear cache and fetch fresh
Installation interrupted by app termination - should resume or cleanup on next launch
Multiple concurrent installItem() calls for same item - should deduplicate or queue
refreshRegistry() called while loadRegistry() in progress - should cancel and restart
Device goes offline during installation - should pause and resume when online
Registry response contains items with duplicate IDs - should deduplicate by ID
Cache TTL expires exactly during loadRegistry() - should fetch fresh data
Very large registry response causes memory pressure - should stream parse if needed
User force quits during uninstallItem() - should cleanup partial state on next launch
failure_modes: Network timeout after all retries - set error to networkError, show cached data if available

Cache database locked by another process - set error to cacheError, fetch from network
Installation directory not writable - set error to installationError, show permission guidance
Downloaded item fails signature verification - set error to validationError, do not install

Memory leaks possible if Task references create retain cycles
Offline detection may be unreliable on certain network configurations
Error message quality depends on underlying component error granularity
mitigations: Extract complex logic to private helper methods with single responsibility
Use actor isolation or explicit locking for concurrent state access
Use weak self in Task closures and explicit task cancellation
Supplement NWPathMonitor with actual network request failure detection
Define rich error types in dependencies with context for user-friendly messages
risk_register.blast_radius: Medium - coordinator is central facade so bugs affect all registry UI. However, fallback to cache limits user-facing impact. Individual components (fetcher, cache, installer) remain functional independently.
risk_register.fallback_plan: If coordinator design proves inadequate, UI can temporarily bypass coordinator and call fetcher/cache/installer directly. This is not recommended long-term but provides escape hatch during development.

atom_description: Implement PluginsSelectionView.swift as a SwiftUI view that renders plugins from RegistryManager grouped by their forCli property (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI sections). The view includes a search bar for filtering by name/description, category filter chips, LazyVGrid layout for plugin cards, selection state management via Binding to Set of PluginItem, and visual feedback for installed vs available plugins. Each plugin card displays name, description, version, author, download count, and an install/selected toggle button.
problem_statement: Users need a visual interface to discover and select plugins from the remote extension registry during onboarding. Without a dedicated plugins view grouped by CLI, users cannot easily find plugins compatible with their installed CLI tools. The view must handle potentially hundreds of plugins efficiently with search, filtering, and lazy loading.

story_description: Create the foundational data model and types for representing hook execution events in a timeline/Gantt chart format, enabling visualization of hook lifecycles with proper temporal relationships and hierarchical structure.
task_description: Define the core HookTimelineEvent struct and supporting enums (HookTimelineCategory, HookTimelineStatus) that represent individual hook execution events with start/end times, nesting depth, parent-child relationships, and execution status for Gantt visualization.
atom_description: Implement the HookTimelineEvent struct with UUID-based identification, name, category enum, start/end Date timestamps, depth integer for nesting level, recursive children array, and status enum. Also implement HookTimelineCategory enum with session/turn/tool/file/git cases and HookTimelineStatus enum with pending/running/completed/failed/cancelled cases.
problem_statement: The Hooks Builder currently displays hook executions in a flat list format without temporal context. Users cannot visualize when hooks started, how long they ran, which hooks ran concurrently, or understand parent-child relationships between session-level and tool-level hooks. A Gantt-style visualization requires a structured timeline event model that captures start time, duration, nesting depth, and hierarchical relationships.

Static factory methods for creating events from HookExecution objects

Persistence or serialization of timeline events

SwiftUI is available as the UI framework and Identifiable protocol is required for ForEach rendering
UUID is acceptable as the identifier type for timeline events
Date arithmetic for duration calculation uses standard Foundation APIs
Child events always have start times after or equal to parent start times
Maximum nesting depth is bounded by practical limits (typically 3-4 levels: session > turn > tool > file)
constraints: Must be a value type (struct) for SwiftUI state management and copy-on-write semantics
Must conform to Identifiable with UUID for stable ForEach identity
Recursive children array must not create reference cycles (struct ensures this)
Category colors are defined externally in theme constants, not hardcoded in model
All Date properties use system timezone, no UTC conversion required
Status transitions follow state machine rules: pending -> running -> completed/failed/cancelled
Maximum nesting depth is 3 levels (session -> turn -> tool)
Depth property must be clamped to 0-2 range (0=session, 1=turn, 2=tool)

FR2: HookTimelineCategory enum shall define cases session, turn, tool, file, git each mapping to a semantic color role
FR3: HookTimelineStatus enum shall define cases pending, running, completed, failed, cancelled representing execution lifecycle states

FR5: HookTimelineEvent shall provide duration computed property returning TimeInterval or nil if endTime is nil
FR6: HookTimelineEvent shall provide isActive computed property returning true if status is pending or running
FR7: HookTimelineEvent shall provide static factory method fromHookExecution(_ execution: HookExecution, depth: Int, children: [HookTimelineEvent]) returning HookTimelineEvent

FR9: HookTimelineStatus shall provide iconName computed property returning SF Symbol name for status indicator

Step 2: Define HookTimelineCategory enum with cases session, turn, tool, file, git and add color computed property returning Color from BlazeTheme

edge_cases: Edge case 1: endTime is nil for currently running hooks - duration returns nil, isActive returns true based on status
Edge case 2: startTime equals endTime for instant hooks - duration returns 0.0 which is valid
Edge case 3: Empty children array for leaf-level events - valid state, no special handling needed
Edge case 4: Deeply nested children (depth > 10) - no hard limit enforced, builder responsible for reasonable depth
Edge case 5: HookExecution with nil startedAt timestamp - factory method returns nil
Edge case 6: Unknown hook type in HookExecution - factory method maps to tool category as default
Edge case 7: Children array contains events with mismatched depth values - no validation at model level, builder responsibility
failure_modes: FM1: Factory method receives HookExecution with nil startedAt - returns nil, caller must handle optional
FM2: Duration calculation on event where endTime precedes startTime (clock skew) - returns negative TimeInterval which may confuse UI, recommend abs() wrapper in display layer
FM3: Memory pressure from very large children arrays - struct copy-on-write helps but recommend limiting children count in builder
FM4: Category color lookup fails if BlazeTheme not initialized - provide fallback Color.gray in color computed property

story_description: Create the foundational data model and types for representing hook execution events in a timeline/Gantt chart format, enabling visualization of hook lifecycles with proper temporal relationships and hierarchical structure.
task_description: Implement the HookTimelineBuilder struct that converts raw HookExecution arrays into hierarchical HookTimelineEvent trees suitable for Gantt visualization, supporting both turn-level and session-level view modes with provider-agnostic event normalization.
atom_description: Implement HookTimelineBuilder struct with static factory methods buildTurnTimeline and buildSessionTimeline that transform HookExecution arrays into HookTimelineEvent hierarchies. Include normalizeEventType method for mapping provider-specific event names (Claude PreToolUse, Gemini tool_call_start, Codex exec_start) to unified HookTimelineCategory enum values. Handle parent-child relationship construction, depth calculation, and time range normalization.
problem_statement: The Gantt visualization requires transforming flat HookExecution arrays from HookStore into hierarchical HookTimelineEvent trees. Raw execution data lacks parent-child relationships, normalized categories, and proper nesting depth. Different providers (Claude, Gemini, Codex) emit different event type names that must be mapped to a unified category system. The builder must construct timeline hierarchies for both single-turn views (hooks within one prompt-response cycle) and session-level views (turns as parents containing their hooks).

constraints: Must be a value type (struct) with only static methods for stateless, testable design
Must not retain references to HookExecution or HookStore (pure transformation)
Must handle empty execution arrays gracefully returning empty result arrays
Must handle executions with nil startedAt by filtering them out (not crashing)
Must handle executions with nil completedAt (still running) by leaving endTime nil in result
Maximum depth enforced at 10 levels to prevent runaway recursion
Provider event mapping must be extensible for future providers without breaking existing logic
Time complexity should be O(n log n) or better where n is execution count
functional_requirements: FR1: HookTimelineBuilder shall be a struct with no stored properties and only static methods
FR2: buildTurnTimeline shall accept (executions: [HookExecution], turnStart: Date, turnEnd: Date?) and return [HookTimelineEvent] representing hooks within that turn boundary
FR3: buildSessionTimeline shall accept (executions: [HookExecution], turns: [TurnBoundary]) and return [HookTimelineEvent] with TurnBoundary events as parents and hooks as children
FR4: normalizeEventType shall accept (rawType: String, provider: EngineType) and return HookTimelineCategory mapping provider event names to unified categories
FR5: Builder shall filter out HookExecution objects where startedAt is nil and log a warning
FR6: Builder shall calculate depth based on temporal containment: if child.startTime >= parent.startTime and (child.endTime <= parent.endTime or parent.endTime is nil), child depth = parent.depth + 1
FR7: Builder shall sort output events by startTime ascending within each depth level
FR8: Builder shall map HookExecution.outcome to HookTimelineStatus (success -> completed, failure -> failed, etc.)
FR9: Builder shall limit maximum depth to 10 and flatten any deeper events to depth 10 with warning log
FR10: normalizeEventType shall return .tool as default for unknown event types
nonfunctional_requirements: NFR1: buildTurnTimeline shall process 100 executions in under 10 milliseconds on M1 hardware
NFR2: buildSessionTimeline shall process 1000 executions across 50 turns in under 100 milliseconds
NFR3: Memory allocation during build shall not exceed 2x the output array size
NFR4: Builder methods shall be thread-safe (no shared mutable state)
NFR5: All public methods shall have documentation comments describing parameters and return values
implementation_steps: Step 1: Create new file HookTimelineBuilder.swift in Blaze/Sources/Core/HookTimeline/ directory
Step 2: Define TurnBoundary struct with properties: id (UUID with default UUID()), turnNumber (Int), startTime (Date), endTime (Date?), promptPreview (String?)
Step 3: Add Identifiable conformance to TurnBoundary
Step 4: Define HookTimelineBuilder struct as empty struct (no stored properties)
Step 5: Implement private static helper filterValidExecutions(_ executions: [HookExecution]) -> [HookExecution] that removes entries with nil startedAt
Step 6: Implement private static helper sortByStartTime(_ executions: [HookExecution]) -> [HookExecution] using sorted(by:) on startedAt
Step 7: Implement private static helper mapOutcomeToStatus(_ outcome: HookOutcome) -> HookTimelineStatus with switch mapping success->completed, failure->failed, timeout->failed, pending->running
Step 8: Implement static func normalizeEventType(rawType: String, provider: EngineType) -> HookTimelineCategory with switch on provider then rawType pattern matching
Step 9: Add Claude event mappings in normalizeEventType: PreToolUse/PostToolUse -> .tool, UserPromptSubmit/Stop -> .turn, SessionStart/PreCompact -> .session
Step 10: Add Gemini event mappings: tool_call_start/tool_call_end -> .tool, prompt_start/response_end -> .turn, session_init -> .session
Step 11: Add Codex event mappings: exec_start/exec_complete -> .tool, sandbox_enter/sandbox_exit -> .session
Step 12: Add default case in normalizeEventType returning .tool with debug log for unknown types
Step 13: Implement private static helper buildHierarchy(from executions: [HookExecution], depth: Int, parentStart: Date, parentEnd: Date?) -> [HookTimelineEvent] using recursive temporal containment
Step 14: In buildHierarchy, cap depth at 10 and log warning if exceeded

Step 15: Implement static func buildTurnTimeline(executions: [HookExecution], turnStart: Date, turnEnd: Date?) -> [HookTimelineEvent] calling filterValidExecutions, sortByStartTime, then buildHierarchy with depth 0

Step 16: Implement static func buildSessionTimeline(executions: [HookExecution], turns: [TurnBoundary]) -> [HookTimelineEvent] creating parent events for each TurnBoundary and calling buildTurnTimeline for children
Step 17: Add documentation comments to all public types and methods
Step 18: Write unit tests covering all public methods and edge cases

edge_cases: Edge case 1: Empty executions array - returns empty HookTimelineEvent array without error
Edge case 2: All executions have nil startedAt - returns empty array after filtering, logs warning for each filtered execution
Edge case 3: Single execution with nil completedAt (still running) - returns single event with endTime nil and status .running
Edge case 4: Deeply nested executions exceeding depth 10 - flattens to depth 10 and logs warning message
Edge case 5: Executions with overlapping time ranges but no clear parent-child relationship - placed at same depth level sorted by startTime
Edge case 6: TurnBoundary array is empty in buildSessionTimeline - returns empty array (no parent events to attach hooks to)
Edge case 7: Execution startTime is after turnEnd - excluded from turn timeline (out of bounds)
Edge case 8: Unknown provider event type string - mapped to .tool category as fallback with debug log
Edge case 9: Clock skew causing endTime before startTime - event created with negative duration (display layer handles)
Edge case 10: Very large execution array (10000+ items) - performance may degrade but should not crash
failure_modes: FM1: HookExecution.startedAt force unwrap crash - prevented by filterValidExecutions removing nil entries before processing
FM2: Infinite recursion in buildHierarchy - prevented by depth cap at 10 levels
FM3: Memory exhaustion from large arrays - mitigated by streaming/lazy evaluation in future if needed, current design accepts 2x memory overhead
FM4: Race condition if HookExecution array mutated during build - prevented by accepting array by value (copy semantics)
FM5: Provider enum mismatch causing wrong event mapping - normalizeEventType has catch-all default case returning .tool

story_description: Create the foundational data model, builder logic, and view model for representing hook execution events in a timeline/Gantt chart format, enabling visualization of hook lifecycles with proper temporal relationships, hierarchical structure, and real-time updates.
task_description: Create the HookGanttViewModel ObservableObject that manages timeline state, coordinates data fetching from HookStore, handles view mode switching between turn and session views, tracks expand/collapse state, computes derived metrics (time range, duration, hook count), and subscribes to real-time hook execution updates.
atom_description: Implement HookGanttViewModel as a MainActor-isolated ObservableObject with published properties for viewMode (HookGanttViewMode enum), timelineEvents array, selectedEvent optional, expandedEventIds set, and isLoading state. Add computed properties for timeRange, totalDuration, and hookCount. Implement data loading from HookStore, real-time observation via Combine publishers, and expand/collapse toggle methods.
problem_statement: The Gantt visualization requires a reactive state management layer that bridges the data model (HookTimelineEvent from G001) and builder logic (HookTimelineBuilder from G002) with the SwiftUI views (G004-G007). Without a dedicated ViewModel, views would need to manage complex state like expand/collapse tracking, mode switching, real-time subscriptions, and derived metric calculations directly, violating separation of concerns and making the UI code unmaintainable.

Real-time update: HookRunner emits execution, ViewModel receives via subscription, updates timelineEvents, view animates new bar
Load on appear: View appears, calls loadTimeline(), ViewModel fetches data, view transitions from loading to loaded
edge_cases: Edge case 1: No hook executions exist for session - timelineEvents empty, timeRange returns Date() to Date() (empty closed range), totalDuration returns 0, hookCount returns 0
Edge case 2: Session ID is nil - load all executions across all sessions (global view)
Edge case 3: HookStore.getExecutions throws error - catch and set timelineEvents to empty, log error, do not crash
Edge case 4: switchMode called while loadTimeline is in progress - should cancel previous load or queue (use Task cancellation)
Edge case 5: toggleExpanded called for non-existent eventId - no-op, Set handles gracefully
Edge case 6: selectEvent called with event not in timelineEvents - still set selectedEvent (view handles mismatch)
Edge case 7: Real-time execution arrives for different session than current sessionId filter - ignore if sessionId filter is active
Edge case 8: startObserving called multiple times - should not create duplicate subscriptions (check cancellables.isEmpty or use single subscription)
Edge case 9: stopObserving called when no subscriptions exist - no-op, cancellables.removeAll() is safe on empty set
Edge case 10: deinit called while async loadTimeline is in progress - Task should be cancelled to prevent accessing deallocated self

risks: Risk 1: MainActor isolation may cause unexpected deadlocks if async helpers are not properly nonisolated
Risk 2: Combine subscription may leak if deinit is not called (e.g., ViewModel held by closure)

Mitigation 5: Implement ViewModel with mock publisher first; HookRunner modification is small (single property addition)

story_description: Create the visual components for rendering hook execution events in a Gantt chart format, enabling users to see hook timelines with proper visual hierarchy, expandable rows, and interactive elements.
task_description: Build the GanttRow SwiftUI view that renders a single hook timeline event as a horizontal row containing the hook name label, expand/collapse chevron for children, and an embedded GanttBar showing the execution timeline with proper indentation based on nesting depth.
atom_description: Implement GanttRow.swift as a SwiftUI View that displays a single HookTimelineEvent row within the Gantt chart. The row contains a leading label area with hook name, category icon, expand/collapse chevron (if children exist), and a trailing GanttBar component positioned according to the event's start/end times relative to the visible time range. Supports indentation based on depth property and propagates selection/expansion callbacks to parent view.
problem_statement: The Hook Gantt Visualization feature requires a reusable row component that renders individual hook timeline events. Each row must display the hook name with proper indentation based on hierarchy depth, show an expand/collapse chevron when children exist, render the category-colored timeline bar at the correct horizontal position, and support hover/click interactions. Without this component, the HookGanttView cannot render the timeline list.

story_description: Create the foundational data model and types for representing hook execution events in a timeline/Gantt chart format, enabling visualization of hook lifecycles with proper temporal relationships and hierarchical structure.
task_description: Create the GanttBar SwiftUI view component that renders an individual animated timeline bar representing a hook execution event, with proper width calculation based on duration, color coding by category, status indicators, and smooth animations for running state.
atom_description: Implement the GanttBar SwiftUI view that displays a horizontal bar representing a hook execution event. The bar width is proportional to event duration relative to total timeline span. Bar color is derived from HookTimelineCategory. Running events display a pulsing animation. Completed events show solid fill. Failed events show red tint with error icon. Bar supports hover state for tooltip trigger and tap for selection.
problem_statement: The Gantt visualization requires individual bar components that visually represent hook execution events on a timeline. Users need to see at a glance: how long each hook took (bar width), what type of hook it was (color), whether it succeeded or failed (status indicator), and which hooks are currently running (animation). Without a dedicated GanttBar component, the timeline would be static and uninformative.

The tooltip appears on mouse hover over Gantt bars and rows.
atom_description: Implement the HookTooltip SwiftUI view component that renders a floating popover-style tooltip when hovering over GanttBar or GanttRow elements. The tooltip displays: hook name with icon, execution status with color indicator, start time formatted as HH:mm:ss.SSS, duration in human-readable format (e.g., 142ms, 1.2s), hook type badge (command/prompt), input JSON preview (first 200 chars), output/result preview (first 200 chars), environment variables accessed, and error message with stack trace preview for failed hooks. Uses NSPopover on macOS for native tooltip behavior with smooth fade animations.
problem_statement: When users view the Gantt timeline, they can see hook execution bars with colors indicating status, but they lack detailed context about what each hook actually did. Users need to hover over a bar to see: what hook ran, how long it took, what input it received, what output it produced, which environment variables it accessed, and why it failed (if applicable). Without tooltips, users must navigate away from the Gantt view to inspect individual hook details, breaking their flow and reducing the utility of the visualization.

story_description: Establish foundational communication layer between Blaze and the Codex app-server daemon, enabling JSON-RPC based interaction for advanced scenarios where the app-server mode provides better session management and event streaming than direct CLI invocation.
task_description: Create CodexAppServerAdapter class that handles JSON-RPC 2.0 communication with the Codex app-server daemon, including connection management, request/response serialization, notification handling, and error propagation.
atom_description: Implement CodexAppServerAdapter actor conforming to EngineAdapter protocol with JSON-RPC 2.0 client capabilities over HTTP transport, including request ID generation, response correlation, notification stream handling, and comprehensive error types for connection failures, timeouts, and protocol errors.
problem_statement: Codex CLI can run in app-server mode which provides a persistent daemon process with JSON-RPC interface. This offers advantages over direct CLI spawning: persistent sessions, better event streaming, and reduced process overhead. However, Blaze currently has no adapter to communicate with this mode. We need a robust JSON-RPC client adapter that can connect to the app-server, send requests, receive responses, and handle the bidirectional notification stream for real-time updates.
scope_in: CodexAppServerAdapter actor definition conforming to EngineAdapter protocol
JSON-RPC 2.0 request message structure (id, method, params)
JSON-RPC 2.0 response message structure (id, result, error)
JSON-RPC 2.0 notification message structure (method, params, no id)
HTTP transport layer using URLSession for request/response
Server-Sent Events (SSE) transport for notification stream
Request ID generation using atomic counter or UUID
Response correlation mapping pending requests to completions
Connection state management (disconnected, connecting, connected, error)
Error types for connection refused, timeout, invalid response, RPC error
Async/await API surface for all RPC calls
AsyncSequence for notification events
scope_out: App-server process lifecycle management (covered in X002-MANAGER)
Event stream parsing and normalization (covered in X003-EVENTS)
Session persistence and state management (covered in X004-SESSION)
Port discovery and configuration (covered in X005-CONFIG)
Authentication and authorization mechanisms
WebSocket transport (app-server uses HTTP + SSE)
Reconnection logic with backoff (managed by lifecycle manager)
Request batching or pipelining
assumptions: Codex app-server runs on localhost at a configurable port (default 3333)
App-server implements JSON-RPC 2.0 specification over HTTP POST
App-server provides SSE endpoint for notification streaming at /events
All communication is unencrypted over localhost (no TLS required)
App-server is single-tenant, no multi-user authentication needed
Response timeout of 30 seconds is acceptable for most operations
URLSession is appropriate for HTTP transport (no need for custom networking)
Swift Concurrency (async/await, actors) is the preferred concurrency model
constraints: Must conform to existing EngineAdapter protocol for integration with SessionStore
Actor isolation required to prevent data races on connection state
All network operations must be cancellable via Task cancellation
Error messages must be user-readable for display in UI
No third-party dependencies allowed; use Foundation networking only
Must support macOS 13.0+ (Ventura) minimum deployment target
JSON encoding/decoding must handle all Codable types in request params
Notification stream must not block the main thread
functional_requirements: FR1: CodexAppServerAdapter shall conform to EngineAdapter protocol with async methods for submit, cancel, and event stream
FR2: Adapter shall implement JSON-RPC 2.0 request format with id (String), jsonrpc (literal 2.0), method (String), params (Encodable?)
FR3: Adapter shall parse JSON-RPC 2.0 response format with id, result (Decodable), or error (code, message, data)
FR4: Adapter shall maintain a dictionary mapping request IDs to CheckedContinuation for response correlation
FR5: Adapter shall generate unique request IDs using UUID().uuidString for each outgoing request
FR6: Adapter shall provide connect() async throws method to establish HTTP connection and verify server availability
FR7: Adapter shall provide disconnect() method to close connections and cancel pending requests
FR8: Adapter shall expose connectionState: ConnectionState published property for UI binding
FR9: Adapter shall provide call<T: Decodable>(method: String, params: Encodable?) async throws -> T for generic RPC calls
FR10: Adapter shall provide notifications: AsyncStream<JSONRPCNotification> property for incoming notifications
FR11: Adapter shall timeout requests after configurable duration (default 30 seconds) with TimeoutError
FR12: Adapter shall propagate JSON-RPC error responses as CodexRPCError with code, message, and optional data
nonfunctional_requirements: NFR1: Request round-trip latency shall be under 100ms for local requests (excluding server processing)
NFR2: Adapter shall support at least 10 concurrent pending requests without degradation
NFR3: Memory footprint of adapter instance shall not exceed 1MB excluding response buffers
NFR4: Notification stream shall deliver events within 50ms of server emission
NFR5: Connection establishment shall complete within 5 seconds or fail with timeout
NFR6: Adapter shall gracefully handle server disconnect without crashing

edge_cases: Edge case 1: Server not running when connect() called - throws connectionFailed with ECONNREFUSED underlying error
Edge case 2: Server crashes mid-request - pending continuation resumed with serverDisconnected error
Edge case 3: Response received for unknown request ID - logged as warning, response discarded
Edge case 4: Malformed JSON in response body - throws invalidResponse with parsing error details
Edge case 5: Server returns JSON-RPC error response - throws rpcError with code and message
Edge case 6: Request cancelled by Task cancellation - continuation cancelled, request removed from pending
Edge case 7: Multiple rapid connect() calls - only first proceeds, subsequent await first completion
Edge case 8: SSE stream interrupted - notification continuation finishes, triggers reconnect via manager
Edge case 9: Very large response body (over 10MB) - handled by URLSession memory limits, may fail
Edge case 10: Server returns success response with null result - decoded as nil, valid for void methods
failure_modes: FM1: ECONNREFUSED on connect - display Connection refused error with suggestion to start app-server
FM2: Request timeout after 30 seconds - display timeout error, allow retry
FM3: JSON decode failure - display Invalid response from server with raw response in logs
FM4: RPC error code -32600 (Invalid Request) - display Server rejected request, check parameters
FM5: RPC error code -32601 (Method not found) - display Method not supported by app-server version
FM6: RPC error code -32603 (Internal error) - display Server internal error, check server logs
FM7: SSL/TLS error (if HTTPS attempted) - should not occur on localhost, fallback to HTTP
FM8: Memory pressure during large response - URLSession handles, may receive didReceiveMemoryWarning

story_description: Implement reliable lifecycle management for the Codex CLI app-server daemon including startup, health monitoring, graceful shutdown, and automatic restart capabilities to ensure consistent communication between the Blaze harness and the Codex backend.
task_description: Create a Swift actor responsible for starting, stopping, monitoring, and restarting the Codex CLI app-server process with health checks, timeout handling, and state transitions exposed via async/await APIs.
atom_description: Implement CodexAppServerManager actor in Blaze/Sources/Engine/CodexAppServerManager.swift providing full lifecycle control for the Codex app-server daemon. The manager handles process spawning via Foundation.Process, port allocation, health check polling via HTTP GET to /health endpoint, graceful SIGTERM shutdown with SIGKILL fallback, automatic restart on crash detection, and state machine transitions (stopped, starting, running, stopping, error). Exposes async methods start(), stop(), restart(), and observable @Published state for UI binding.
problem_statement: The Blaze harness needs to communicate with Codex CLI via its app-server mode for advanced scenarios like persistent sessions and structured event streaming. Without a dedicated lifecycle manager, the app would have to manually spawn processes, track PIDs, handle crashes, and coordinate shutdown - all error-prone operations that belong in a single responsible component. The manager must handle the daemon lifecycle reliably across app launches, backgrounding, and unexpected terminations.

story_description: Establish foundational communication layer between Blaze and the Codex app-server daemon, enabling JSON-RPC based interaction for advanced scenarios where the app-server mode provides better session management and event streaming than direct CLI invocation.
task_description: Create CodexAppServerEvents module responsible for parsing the Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream from the Codex app-server daemon, normalizing raw events into the NormalizedEvent type consumed by the UI layer, and handling stream lifecycle including reconnection state and buffering.
atom_description: Implement CodexAppServerEvents actor in Blaze/Sources/Engine/CodexAppServerEvents.swift providing comprehensive SSE stream parsing for the Codex app-server notification channel. The module receives raw SSE data lines from the adapter layer, parses event type and data fields per SSE specification, deserializes JSON payloads into strongly-typed Codex event structs, maps Codex-specific event types to the shared NormalizedEvent enum for UI consumption, handles malformed events gracefully with logging, manages event buffering during reconnection, and exposes an AsyncSequence-based API for downstream consumers. Supports all Codex app-server event types including prompt_started, token_generated, tool_call_started, tool_call_completed, error_occurred, and session_ended.
problem_statement: The Codex app-server emits real-time events via Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream to notify clients of ongoing activity such as token generation, tool invocations, and errors. The raw SSE stream contains untyped JSON payloads with Codex-specific field names and structures that differ from our unified NormalizedEvent schema used by the UI layer. Without a dedicated parsing and normalization layer, the adapter would need to embed parsing logic, the UI would need Codex-specific handling, and error recovery would be inconsistent. We need a focused event stream parser that translates the raw SSE stream into a clean AsyncSequence of NormalizedEvents that the rest of the application can consume uniformly.

edge_cases: EC-01: Empty data field in SSE event - skip event with debug log, do not yield
EC-02: Missing event type field - default to message type per SSE spec
EC-03: Malformed JSON in data field - log warning with first 200 chars of data, skip event
EC-04: Unknown event type string - parse as unknown(String) variant, normalize to generic event
EC-05: Event ID with special characters - store as-is for reconnection header
EC-06: Retry field present - log but ignore (retry logic in adapter layer)
EC-07: Very large data field over 1MB - attempt parse, may fail with memory error, skip
EC-08: Data split across multiple data: lines - accumulate correctly with newlines preserved
EC-09: Rapid event burst over 1000/sec - apply backpressure via AsyncStream buffer
EC-10: Consumer slower than producer - AsyncStream buffers, may drop if buffer limit policy set
EC-11: Stream interrupted mid-event - discard incomplete pending data on reset
EC-12: Empty line before any data - ignore, do not emit empty event
EC-13: Comment lines interspersed - skip comment lines, continue accumulation
EC-14: Timestamp in future - clamp to current time with warning
EC-15: Timestamp is zero - use current time as fallback with warning
EC-16: Tool arguments contain nested JSON - AnyCodable preserves structure correctly
failure_modes: FM-01: JSON decode failure - log warning with event type and error, skip event, continue processing
FM-02: Unknown event type - normalize to generic NormalizedEvent.unknown variant, log info
FM-03: Buffer overflow during extended reconnection - drop oldest events, log warning with count dropped
FM-04: Continuation already finished - check before yield, log error if attempting to yield to finished stream
FM-05: Actor reentrancy during rapid feed() calls - actor isolation prevents, but log if detected
FM-06: Memory pressure from large events - rely on system memory warnings, no custom handling
FM-07: Invalid UTF-8 in SSE line - String initializer handles, log warning if lossy conversion
FM-08: Extremely long line without newline - URLSession line reading handles, may split

story_description: Establish foundational communication layer between Blaze and the Codex app-server daemon, enabling JSON-RPC based interaction for advanced scenarios where the app-server mode provides better session management and event streaming than direct CLI invocation.
task_description: Create CodexAppServerSession actor that manages session state persistence for Codex app-server mode, including conversation history, context windows, checkpoint creation, recovery from crashes, and synchronization between Blaze local state and app-server daemon state.
atom_description: Implement CodexAppServerSession actor in Blaze/Sources/Engine/CodexAppServerSession.swift providing session state management for persistent Codex app-server mode. The actor handles session ID generation and tracking, conversation history buffering with token counting, context window management with sliding window and summarization triggers, checkpoint creation to SQLite for crash recovery, state reconciliation between Blaze and app-server on reconnect, session metadata storage (creation time, last activity, token usage), and integration with SessionStore for unified session view across all engine types.
problem_statement: When Blaze uses Codex in app-server mode, session state lives in two places: the long-running app-server daemon process and the Blaze harness. Unlike headless CLI mode where each invocation is stateless, app-server maintains conversation context across multiple requests. This creates synchronization challenges: what happens if Blaze crashes and restarts? What if the app-server crashes? What if both restart? We need a session persistence layer that keeps Blaze state synchronized with app-server state, enables crash recovery, and provides a unified view of session history regardless of where the authoritative state lives.

Session ID generation using UUID for new sessions and retrieval of existing IDs from app-server

Checkpoint creation on configurable intervals and before risky operations
Checkpoint storage in SQLite via SessionStore with session_id, checkpoint_data, created_at columns

State reconciliation protocol comparing Blaze checkpoint with app-server reported history

Integration with SessionStore for CRUD operations on session records

Handling of app-server session ID mismatch (app-server restarted with different session)
Graceful handling of checkpoint corruption with fallback to fresh session

assumptions: App-server provides method to query current session ID and conversation history length
App-server session ID is stable across requests within same daemon lifetime
App-server restarts create new session ID, requiring Blaze-side recovery flow
SQLite database is available via SessionStore for checkpoint persistence
Checkpoints under 10MB are acceptable for SQLite blob storage
Checkpoint creation completes within 500ms for typical session sizes
Token counting algorithm matches OpenAI tokenizer closely enough for context management
App-server reports token usage in response metadata for tracking
Session recovery should complete within 2 seconds for good UX
User prefers to continue previous session rather than start fresh after crash
constraints: Must conform to existing EngineSession protocol for integration with session infrastructure
Actor isolation required to prevent data races on session state mutations
All public methods must be async for non-blocking operation
Checkpoint data must be JSON serializable using Codable
Must not block main thread during checkpoint creation or recovery
Session metadata must be queryable without loading full checkpoint data
Must handle concurrent requests to same session without corruption
Token count must be estimated quickly (under 10ms for 10K tokens)
Must degrade gracefully when app-server is unreachable during reconciliation
Must not lose user data even on unclean shutdown (checkpoint on every user message)

edge_cases: Edge case 01: Session created but no messages added - checkpoint contains empty history array but valid metadata
Edge case 02: Checkpoint file corrupted or truncated - log error, notify delegate, start fresh session with warning
Edge case 03: App-server session ID differs from checkpoint - server restarted, log warning, continue with Blaze history as source of truth
Edge case 04: App-server has more messages than Blaze - messages sent via direct CLI, attempt to fetch and merge
Edge case 05: Blaze has more messages than app-server - messages lost in server restart, Blaze history is authoritative
Edge case 06: Extremely long message exceeding token estimate buffer - clamp to reasonable estimate, log warning
Edge case 07: Checkpoint version newer than code supports - reject with clear error, suggest app update
Edge case 08: Checkpoint version older than current - run migration chain to update format
Edge case 09: Concurrent checkpoint writes from rapid message appends - serialize writes via actor isolation
Edge case 10: SessionStore database locked by another process - retry with backoff, fail after 5 attempts
Edge case 11: Disk full during checkpoint write - catch error, notify user, continue without checkpoint
Edge case 12: Session metadata dates in future due to clock skew - normalize to current time if future
Edge case 13: Token count estimation overflow for huge messages - use Int64 internally, cap display values
Edge case 14: Zero-length message content - allow but skip token counting, log debug message
Edge case 15: Unicode normalization affecting token count - use NFC normalized form for consistency
failure_modes: FM-01: Checkpoint write failure due to disk error - continue session in memory, retry checkpoint on next interval, warn user of unsaved state
FM-02: Checkpoint read failure on recovery - start fresh session, log detailed error, offer to view corrupted data
FM-03: Reconciliation timeout (app-server unresponsive) - continue with local state, retry reconciliation on next message
FM-04: Token estimation wildly inaccurate - may hit actual limit unexpectedly, rely on server error response as fallback
FM-05: Database schema mismatch after update - migration should handle, but fail clearly if migration missing
FM-06: Memory pressure during large session load - session actor is lazy loaded, checkpoint data streamed if needed
FM-07: Delegate callback throws - catch and log, do not propagate to session actor to prevent state corruption
FM-08: Actor reentrancy during checkpoint - prevented by actor isolation, but test explicitly for this case
rollback_plan: Delete Blaze/Sources/Engine/CodexAppServerSession.swift and Tests/Engine/CodexAppServerSessionTests.swift. Remove SessionStore.saveCheckpoint and loadCheckpoint methods. Drop checkpoints table via migration v9 with DROP TABLE IF EXISTS checkpoints. Remove imports and references from adapter and manager files. User session data in checkpoints table is lost but can be manually exported before rollback if needed. Core session functionality via SessionStore sessions table is unaffected.

story_description: Establish foundational communication layer between Blaze and the Codex app-server daemon, enabling JSON-RPC based interaction for advanced scenarios where the app-server mode provides better session management and event streaming than direct CLI invocation.
task_description: Create CodexAppServerConfig struct and associated configuration management for port allocation, authentication settings, startup parameters, timeout values, and environment variables needed to launch and connect to the Codex app-server daemon.
atom_description: Implement CodexAppServerConfig struct in Blaze/Sources/Engine/CodexAppServerConfig.swift providing strongly-typed configuration for the Codex app-server daemon including port range allocation, authentication token retrieval, startup command arguments, timeout values for connection and health checks, environment variable injection, TLS settings for secure connections, and persistence via UserDefaults with Codable serialization. Configuration validates port ranges, provides sensible defaults, and exposes SwiftUI-bindable properties for the settings UI.
problem_statement: The Codex app-server daemon requires multiple configuration parameters to launch correctly: port number, authentication tokens, environment variables, timeout values, and startup flags. Without centralized configuration management, these settings would be scattered across the codebase, making it difficult to maintain consistency, validate inputs, persist user preferences, and provide a unified settings UI. A dedicated configuration struct ensures type safety, validation, persistence, and clean API boundaries between the manager, adapter, and UI layers.

edge_cases: Edge case 01: Port 0 specified - validate() returns invalidPort(0) since 0 means any available port which conflicts with explicit configuration
Edge case 02: Port 80 specified (privileged) - validate() returns invalidPort(80) since ports below 1024 require root
Edge case 03: portRangeStart greater than portRangeEnd - validate() returns invalidPortRange with swapped values
Edge case 04: portRangeStart equals portRangeEnd - valid, means single port with no fallback
Edge case 05: Empty host string - validate() returns emptyHost error
Edge case 06: Host with invalid characters (spaces, special chars) - validate() returns invalidHostname with offending host
Edge case 07: Host as IP address (127.0.0.1) - valid, hostname regex allows IP format
Edge case 08: tlsEnabled true but tlsCertificatePath nil - valid, uses system default certificates
Edge case 09: tlsEnabled true with nonexistent certificate path - validate() returns tlsCertificateNotFound
Edge case 10: Environment variable with key PATH - validate() returns restrictedEnvironmentVariable(PATH)
Edge case 11: Environment variable with key HOME - validate() returns restrictedEnvironmentVariable(HOME)
Edge case 12: Environment variable with key DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH - validate() returns restrictedEnvironmentVariable to prevent injection
Edge case 13: Negative timeout value - validate() returns invalidTimeout with negative value
Edge case 14: Zero timeout value - validate() returns invalidTimeout since zero means no timeout which is dangerous
Edge case 15: Extremely large timeout (over max) - validate() returns invalidTimeout with clamping suggestion
Edge case 16: maxRestartAttempts of 0 - valid, means no auto-restart
Edge case 17: UserDefaults contains malformed data - load() returns nil, caller uses defaults
Edge case 18: Keychain access denied by user - apiKeyFromKeychain() throws KeychainError.accessDenied
Edge case 19: Keychain item not found - apiKeyFromKeychain() returns nil (not an error)
Edge case 20: Configuration saved with old schema version - load() handles via Codable migration or returns nil
failure_modes: FM-01: Validation errors on save - UI displays all errors, save blocked until resolved

story: Implement core hook type enum and supporting structures
story_description: As a Blaze developer, I need strongly-typed hook types with validation so that the hooks builder can enforce correct hook configuration and provide helpful guidance to users.
task: Create HookTypes.swift with HookType enum, HookDefinition struct, TemplateVariable, and HookValidationError
task_description: Implement the foundational type system for hooks including the HookType enum with three cases (prompt, command, agent), each with display metadata, default timeouts, and available template variables. Include HookDefinition struct for hook instances with type-specific validation, TemplateVariable for documenting available variables, and HookValidationError for validation feedback.
atom: HookType enum with cases, computed properties, and template variables
atom_description: Define HookType as a String-backed Codable enum with prompt, command, and agent cases. Implement computed properties for displayName, icon (SF Symbol), description, defaultTimeout, and templateVariables. The templateVariables property returns type-specific TemplateVariable arrays documenting available substitution variables for prompt hooks ($TOOL_INPUT, $TOOL_RESULT, $USER_PROMPT, $TRANSCRIPT_PATH) and command hooks ($CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT, $CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, $CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE).
problem_statement: The hooks builder UI needs a type-safe foundation to represent the three hook types supported by Claude Code (prompt, command, agent). Each type has different execution semantics, timeouts, and available template variables. Without this type system, the UI cannot provide accurate guidance, validation, or autocomplete for hook configuration.

story: S001: Core Hook Data Types and Matching
story_description: Implement foundational data structures for hook configuration including pattern matchers that determine when hooks fire based on tool names, event types, or custom patterns. These matchers form the core decision logic enabling hooks to target specific tools or events.
task_description: Create HookMatcher struct and MatcherType enum providing exact, multiple, wildcard, and regex pattern matching capabilities for tool names and events. Include specialized matchers for SessionStart and PreCompact events, plus intelligent pattern suggestions.
atom_description: Implement complete pattern matching infrastructure in HookMatchers.swift including HookMatcher struct with automatic type detection, MatcherType enum with four matching strategies (exact, multiple, wildcard, regex), SessionStartMatcher enum for session lifecycle events, PreCompactMatcher enum for compaction triggers, and MatcherSuggestions helper providing context-aware pattern recommendations.
problem_statement: Hooks need a flexible pattern matching system to determine when they should fire. A hook targeting Write operations should not fire for Read operations. A hook for session startup should not fire on resume. Currently there is no pattern matching infrastructure. We need a comprehensive matcher system that supports exact tool name matching, pipe-delimited multiple tool matching, wildcard matching for all tools, and regex matching for complex patterns like MCP tool namespaces. Additionally, event-specific matchers for SessionStart and PreCompact events require dedicated enum types with semantic meaning.

HookMatcher.matches(_:) method to test if a tool name matches the pattern
SessionStartMatcher enum with startup, resume, clear, and compact cases
PreCompactMatcher enum with manual and auto cases

MatcherSuggestions.suggestions(for:) method returning context-aware patterns

DisplayName and icon properties on MatcherType for UI presentation

assumptions: Pipe character (|) is never used in actual tool names, making it safe as a delimiter
Tool names from Claude Code are stable strings matching documented names
Regex patterns use NSRegularExpression syntax (ICU regular expressions)
All matchers operate synchronously without async requirements
SessionStart event types from CLI match the four defined cases exactly
PreCompact trigger types are limited to manual user action or automatic threshold
constraints: Must use Foundation NSRegularExpression for regex matching, no third-party regex libraries
All types must be Sendable for actor isolation in HookRunner
Regex compilation errors must not crash; invalid patterns should return false for matches
Pattern detection must be deterministic and not depend on external state
All enums must be String-backed for clean JSON serialization
Must support macOS 13.0+ minimum deployment target
No heap allocation in hot path for matches() method where possible
functional_requirements: FR1: HookMatcher shall store pattern as String property accessible for UI display
FR2: HookMatcher shall store type as MatcherType property computed on initialization
FR3: HookMatcher.init(pattern:) shall call MatcherType.detect(from:) to set type automatically
FR4: HookMatcher.matches(_:) shall return true for exact match when type is .exact and pattern equals input
FR5: HookMatcher.matches(_:) shall return true for multiple match when type is .multiple and any pipe-delimited option equals input
FR6: HookMatcher.matches(_:) shall return true unconditionally when type is .wildcard
FR7: HookMatcher.matches(_:) shall return true when type is .regex and pattern matches input via NSRegularExpression
FR8: HookMatcher.matches(_:) shall return false for .regex when pattern is invalid rather than throwing

edge_cases: Edge case 1: Empty pattern string passed to HookMatcher.init - detected as exact, matches only empty string (unusual but valid)
Edge case 2: Pattern with only pipe character | - detected as multiple, splits to empty strings, matches empty tool name
Edge case 3: Pattern asterisk in middle like Read*Write - detected as regex due to *, not wildcard
Edge case 4: Invalid regex pattern like [unclosed - matches() returns false, does not throw
Edge case 5: Pattern with escaped pipe like Read\|Write - detected as regex due to backslash, matches literal Read|Write
Edge case 6: Tool name with special regex characters like mcp__fs__read - matched correctly by exact pattern
Edge case 7: Extremely long pattern (1000+ characters) - may cause regex compilation slowdown, but functions correctly
Edge case 8: Unicode characters in pattern or tool name - handled by NSRegularExpression, matches correctly
Edge case 9: Case sensitivity - matching is case-sensitive, Write does not match write
Edge case 10: Pattern with newlines or whitespace - preserved in pattern, matched literally
failure_modes: FM1: Regex pattern causes catastrophic backtracking - mitigated by NSRegularExpression timeout; matches() may return false after timeout
FM2: Pattern contains characters invalid for JSON encoding - Codable encoding fails; caller must validate input
FM3: MatcherType.detect misclassifies pattern with accidental regex chars - user gets unexpected matches; document detection rules
FM4: SessionStartMatcher raw value changes between versions - JSON deserialization fails for saved configs; maintain backward compatibility

problem_statement: Hooks receive input via stdin as JSON but there is no Swift type to deserialize this input into a strongly-typed struct. Without proper Codable conformance and CodingKeys mapping, the JSON snake_case field names cannot be correctly mapped to Swift camelCase properties. Additionally, tool inputs and results can contain arbitrary JSON structures that need a type-erased wrapper.

story: S001: Define standard output structures for all hook types
story_description: Create a unified output schema that all hooks use to communicate results back to the system, including permission decisions, modified inputs, stop decisions, and system messages.
task: T004: Implement HookOutputSchema.swift with all output types
task_description: Implement the core hook output types including HookOutput struct, HookSpecificOutput, PermissionDecision enum, StopDecision enum, HookExitCode enum, and HookOutputBuilder fluent interface.
atom_description: Implement the full hook output schema with HookOutput as the main return type containing continue flag, suppressOutput flag, optional systemMessage, and hookSpecificOutput for PreToolUse/PermissionRequest hooks. Includes PermissionDecision enum (allow/deny/ask), StopDecision enum (approve/block), HookExitCode enum (success=0, blockingError=2, nonBlockingError=1), and HookOutputBuilder fluent builder pattern.
problem_statement: Hooks need a standardized way to communicate their results back to the system. Without a unified output schema, each hook would define its own return format, leading to parsing complexity, inconsistent behavior, and difficulty in adding new hook types. The output schema must support permission decisions for blocking hooks, input modification for middleware patterns, stop decisions for agent lifecycle control, and system message injection for context augmentation.
scope_in: HookOutput struct with continue, suppressOutput, systemMessage, and hookSpecificOutput fields
HookSpecificOutput struct with permissionDecision, updatedInput, decision, and reason fields
PermissionDecision enum with allow, deny, and ask cases plus displayName, icon, and color computed properties
StopDecision enum with approve and block cases plus displayName computed property
HookExitCode enum with success (0), blockingError (2), and nonBlockingError (1) cases plus description property
HookOutputBuilder fluent interface with continue_, suppressOutput, systemMessage, allow, deny, ask, updatedInput, build, and buildJSON methods
Codable and Sendable conformance for all public types
CaseIterable conformance for PermissionDecision and StopDecision enums

JSONEncoder is available from Foundation for serialization
Swift 5.9 or later with strict concurrency support for Sendable
All hooks will return HookOutput or throw an error
Exit code 2 is reserved for blocking errors per Claude Code convention
constraints: Must conform to Codable for JSON serialization to/from CLI
Must conform to Sendable for safe use in async hook execution
PermissionDecision must match Claude Code expected values (allow/deny/ask)
Exit codes must match Claude Code documentation (0=success, 2=blocking, other=non-blocking)
HookOutputBuilder must use value semantics (copy on write) for thread safety
All string properties must be optional to support partial outputs
functional_requirements: FR1: HookOutput.continue defaults to true and controls whether hook chain processing continues
FR2: HookOutput.suppressOutput defaults to false and controls whether hook output appears in logs
FR3: HookOutput.systemMessage is optional and injects text into Claude system context when present
FR4: HookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision controls automatic approval/rejection of tool calls
FR5: HookSpecificOutput.updatedInput allows hooks to modify tool input before execution (middleware pattern)
FR6: HookSpecificOutput.decision controls whether agent stop is approved or blocked
FR7: HookSpecificOutput.reason provides human-readable explanation for decisions
FR8: PermissionDecision.allow auto-approves the action without user confirmation
FR9: PermissionDecision.deny auto-rejects the action without user confirmation
FR10: PermissionDecision.ask defers to default Claude behavior (prompt user)
FR11: PermissionDecision provides displayName, icon (SF Symbol), and color (hex) for UI rendering
FR12: StopDecision.approve allows the agent to stop normally
FR13: StopDecision.block forces the agent to continue despite stop request
FR14: HookExitCode.success (0) means stdout is shown to Claude
FR15: HookExitCode.blockingError (2) means stderr is returned and processing stops
FR16: HookExitCode.nonBlockingError (1 or other) is logged but processing continues
FR17: HookOutputBuilder.build returns the constructed HookOutput value
FR18: HookOutputBuilder.buildJSON returns pretty-printed sorted JSON string
nonfunctional_requirements: NFR1: All types must be Sendable for safe concurrent access in async contexts
NFR2: JSON encoding must complete in under 1ms for typical outputs
NFR3: Memory footprint must be under 1KB for typical HookOutput instances
NFR4: HookOutputBuilder must support method chaining without heap allocations
NFR5: All enum raw values must be lowercase strings for JSON compatibility

story_description: Provide pre-built hook templates that users can select, customize, and deploy without writing code from scratch, covering common security, testing, logging, context, and workflow patterns.
task_description: Create the HookTemplates Swift module with Template struct, TemplateCategory enum, and five built-in templates: securityFileProtection, securityCommandValidation, testEnforcement, contextLoader, and toolLogger.

problem_statement: Users building hooks from scratch face a steep learning curve: they must understand hook events, output JSON schemas, matcher patterns, and security best practices. Without templates, users either create insecure hooks or avoid the feature entirely. Pre-built templates reduce friction and establish security baselines.

problem_statement: Hook developers need a way to test their hooks before deploying them to production. Currently, testing requires manually crafting JSON input, running scripts in terminal, and parsing output by hand. This is error-prone and slow. A built-in test runner that accepts structured input, executes hooks in isolation, captures all output streams, parses results as HookOutput, and provides clear pass/fail feedback will dramatically improve the hook development experience and reduce broken hook deployments.

edge_cases: Edge case 1: Command string is empty - should throw or return error immediately without spawning process
Edge case 2: Script path contains spaces - must be quoted properly in bash -c argument
Edge case 3: HookInput contains single quotes - must escape as '\'' to prevent shell injection
Edge case 4: Hook script does not exist - process will fail with file not found, captured in stderr
Edge case 5: Hook script is not executable - permission denied error captured in stderr
Edge case 6: Hook outputs invalid JSON - parse fails gracefully, raw output still available in result
Edge case 7: Hook outputs valid JSON but wrong schema - decode fails, error message includes decoding details
Edge case 8: Hook outputs nothing (empty stdout) - parsedOutput is nil, not an error condition
Edge case 9: Hook writes to stderr but exits 0 - success is false because errors array is non-empty
Edge case 10: Hook hangs indefinitely - timeout fires, process terminated, timeout error returned
Edge case 11: Hook exits immediately with non-zero code - failure captured with stderr content
Edge case 12: Temporary file creation fails - throw error from write operation, no cleanup needed
Edge case 13: Multiple concurrent tests - actor isolation ensures each test has independent state
Edge case 14: Process spawn fails - try/catch around process.run() handles launch errors
Edge case 15: Very large stdout output (megabytes) - memory handled by Data, may hit practical limits
failure_modes: FM1: Script not found error - Display: Hook script not found at path. Check: script path and $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR resolution

FM3: Timeout exceeded - Display: Hook execution timed out after N seconds. Suggestion: Increase timeout or optimize hook
FM4: JSON parse failure - Display: Hook output is not valid JSON. Show raw output for debugging
FM5: Process spawn failure - Display: Failed to start hook process. Check system resources and bash availability
FM6: Temporary file write failure - Display: Cannot create temporary script file. Check disk space and permissions
FM7: UTF-8 encoding failure - Display: Hook output contains invalid characters. Check script encoding
FM8: Script crashes or segfaults - Display: Hook process terminated abnormally (signal N). Check script for bugs

story: E005-F009-S002: Implement advanced hook builder view with canvas visualization
story_description: As a power user managing complex hook workflows, I need a visual canvas-based builder that displays hook chains as connected nodes, allowing me to understand the flow of events through triggers, actions, and conditions at a glance, and edit hook configurations through an intuitive node inspector panel.
task: E005-F009-S002-T001: Create AdvancedHookBuilderView with provider selector and canvas controls
task_description: Implement the AdvancedHookBuilderView SwiftUI view that provides a visual hook workflow builder with three-pane layout: node palette on left, interactive canvas in center, and hook inspector panel on right. Include provider selector dropdown (Claude Code, Gemini, Codex disabled), zoom controls with keyboard shortcuts, Test and Export buttons in toolbar, and variable reference panel showing available hook environment variables.
atom_description: Create the AdvancedHookBuilderView.swift file in Blaze/Sources/Settings/Hooks/ that implements the visual hook builder interface. The view uses a three-pane NavigationSplitView layout with: (1) left sidebar containing categorized node palette for event triggers, actions, and conditions, (2) center canvas with pan/zoom gestures rendering hook nodes as cards connected by bezier curves, and (3) right inspector panel showing editable properties for the selected node including name, event type, matcher regex, hook type radio buttons, timeout field, and prompt/command text editor with variable interpolation hints.
problem_statement: The current HooksBuilderView provides basic functionality for creating and editing hooks, but power users need a more sophisticated visual interface that shows hook workflows as connected node graphs. Without this visualization: (1) users cannot easily understand complex multi-step hook chains, (2) users cannot see the flow from event triggers through conditions to actions, (3) users cannot visually identify gaps or misconnections in their hook logic, and (4) users cannot reference available environment variables when writing hook prompts or commands. The AdvancedHookBuilderView addresses these gaps by providing a canvas-based node editor with comprehensive inspector panel.

edge_cases: Edge case 1: Empty pipeline with no nodes - Canvas shows empty state, Test/Export buttons disabled

Edge case 3: Disconnected nodes - Validation warning but not blocking
Edge case 4: Circular connections - Validation error preventing export

Edge case 6: Zoom at minimum scale 0.25 - Zoom out button disabled
Edge case 7: Zoom at maximum scale 4.0 - Zoom in button disabled
Edge case 8: Node dragged off-screen - Canvas pan allows retrieving node

Edge case 11: Provider changed during edit - Warn if hooks incompatible
Edge case 12: Network error loading hooks - Show error message with retry option
Edge case 13: Concurrent edits to same hook - Last write wins, no conflict resolution
Edge case 14: Special characters in command - Properly escaped for bash execution
Edge case 15: Delete last node in pipeline - Returns to empty state

story_description: Enable users to browse, preview, and apply pre-built hook templates from a curated gallery, reducing friction in hook creation by providing battle-tested patterns for common use cases like security validation, testing gates, and logging.
task_description: Create HookTemplateGalleryView SwiftUI component that displays a searchable, filterable gallery of hook templates organized by category with template cards showing metadata, preview capability, and one-click application to the current hook configuration.
atom_description: Implement HookTemplateGalleryView as a SwiftUI view with category filter chips (All, Security, Testing, Logging, Context, Workflow), search bar with real-time filtering, grid layout of template cards displaying name with emoji icon, description, event type, hook type, and Preview/Use Template action buttons.
problem_statement: Creating hooks from scratch requires users to understand hook event schemas, proper JSON structure, shell scripting patterns, and security best practices. This creates high friction for new users and leads to error-prone configurations. Users need a curated gallery of pre-built, tested hook templates they can browse by category, preview before applying, and apply with a single click. The template gallery should make hook creation accessible to users without deep CLI knowledge while providing enough metadata for informed template selection.

story_description: Provide interactive testing and validation capabilities for hook configurations, enabling users to verify hook behavior with sample inputs before deploying to production, reducing trial-and-error debugging cycles.
task_description: Implement HookTestPanelView SwiftUI component that provides an interactive testing interface for hooks with sample input editor, example loaders, test execution, output display with timing metrics, and CLI test command generation.
atom_description: Build HookTestPanelView.swift with JSON input editor featuring syntax highlighting, three example loader buttons (Safe File, Dangerous Path, Custom), Run Test button with execution state, output panel showing formatted JSON response with duration and exit code, and CLI test command generator with copy functionality for terminal reproduction.
problem_statement: Users creating or editing hooks have no way to test them within the Blaze UI. They must manually construct JSON payloads, pipe them to hook scripts via terminal, and interpret raw output. This friction slows hook development and makes it difficult to verify hooks work correctly before enabling them in production sessions. We need an integrated test panel that lets users: (1) edit sample input JSON with syntax highlighting, (2) load predefined examples covering common scenarios, (3) execute the hook and see formatted output with timing, and (4) generate a CLI command to reproduce the test in terminal.

story_description: Provide developers with contextual assistance during hook configuration, including environment variable references, validation feedback, best practices guidance, and interactive testing capabilities to reduce errors and improve hook authoring productivity.
task_description: Create the HookEnvReferenceView SwiftUI component that displays a collapsible panel showing all available Claude Code environment variables (CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT, CLAUDE_ENV_FILE, CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE) with descriptions, usage examples, availability per event type, and copy-to-clipboard buttons for each variable.
atom_description: Implement the HookEnvReferenceView SwiftUI view that renders a collapsible disclosure group containing a reference table of all Claude Code hook environment variables. Each variable row displays: variable name in monospace font, description text, example value, availability tags indicating which hook events can access it, a critical badge for must-use variables, and a copy button that copies the variable reference (e.g., ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}) to the system pasteboard with visual feedback. The panel also includes a Best Practices section with actionable guidance for using environment variables in hook scripts.
problem_statement: Developers creating hook scripts need quick access to available environment variables without leaving the hook builder interface. Currently they must consult external documentation or guess variable names, leading to typos, using unavailable variables in wrong event contexts, and missing best practices like quoting or portable path patterns. An integrated reference panel directly in the hook configuration UI eliminates context switching and provides copy-to-clipboard convenience, reducing errors and improving hook authoring speed.

edge_cases: Edge case 1: UserDefaults corrupted or inaccessible - default to expanded state and continue without persistence
Edge case 2: NSPasteboard.general.setString fails - log warning, do not show confirmation animation, fail silently
Edge case 3: Very long example value that would overflow - text truncates with ellipsis at row boundary
Edge case 4: User taps copy rapidly multiple times - debounce to prevent clipboard spam, each tap resets 1.5s timer
Edge case 5: System in reduced motion mode - skip animation, show checkmark immediately then reset after 1.5s
Edge case 6: VoiceOver active - announce 'Copied' when copy succeeds in addition to visual feedback
Edge case 7: Extremely large Dynamic Type size - variable rows wrap gracefully, copy button remains accessible
Edge case 8: Panel embedded in narrow container less than 200pt - compact layout stacks elements vertically
Edge case 9: Disclosure group expanded but scrolled out of view - state persists correctly when scrolled back
Edge case 10: Dark mode with high contrast enabled - ensure sufficient contrast ratios for all text and badges
failure_modes: FM1: NSPasteboard access denied by sandbox - log error, show alert 'Unable to copy to clipboard', no crash
FM2: UserDefaults write fails - continue with in-memory state only, log warning, no user-visible impact
FM3: Timer for copy confirmation never fires (rare scheduling issue) - stuck in confirmed state until next interaction, not blocking
FM4: Memory pressure during render - panel may render slowly but will complete, no data loss
FM5: Accessibility API unavailable - labels silently ignored, visual UI works normally

story: S002: Hook Validation and Quality Assurance
story_description: Provide comprehensive validation capabilities for hook configurations before export, ensuring configurations are syntactically correct, semantically valid, and follow best practices to prevent runtime failures in Claude Code and other CLI providers.
task_description: Create HookValidator actor that validates HookConfiguration objects, checking for structural errors, missing required fields, invalid patterns, and potential issues that could cause runtime failures or unexpected behavior.
atom_description: Implement HookValidator actor with ValidationResult, ValidationError, and ValidationWarning structs. Provides validate() method for HookConfiguration validation including matcher checks, hook entry validation, and hook definition validation. Includes validateJSON() method for raw JSON syntax checking. Actor isolation ensures thread-safe validation operations.
problem_statement: Hook configurations created in the visual builder or edited manually can contain errors that would cause runtime failures in Claude Code. These include missing required fields, empty hook arrays, invalid matchers, malformed command strings, and incorrect event types. Without pre-export validation, users may deploy broken configurations that fail silently or produce unexpected behavior. We need a comprehensive validator that catches these issues before export and provides actionable error messages.

implementation_steps: Step 1: Create new file HookValidator.swift in Blaze/Sources/Core/Hooks/ directory
Step 2: Import Foundation for JSONSerialization support
Step 3: Declare public actor HookValidator with no stored properties (stateless)
Step 4: Define ValidationResult struct as public and Sendable with isValid, errors, and warnings properties
Step 5: Define ValidationError struct as public Sendable with Identifiable conformance computing id from path plus message
Step 6: Add path (String) and message (String) stored properties to ValidationError
Step 7: Define ValidationWarning struct as public Sendable with Identifiable conformance computing id from path plus message
Step 8: Add path (String) and message (String) stored properties to ValidationWarning
Step 9: Implement public func validate(_ config: HookConfiguration) -> ValidationResult method
Step 10: Initialize empty errors and warnings arrays at method start
Step 11: Iterate over config.hooks dictionary using for (event, entries) in config.hooks pattern
Step 12: For each entry, construct base path as hooks.{event}[{index}]
Step 13: Check if entry.matcher.isEmpty and append warning about matching all if true
Step 14: Check if entry.hooks.isEmpty and append error about no hooks defined if true
Step 15: Iterate over entry.hooks with enumerated() to get hook index
Step 16: Construct hook path as {basePath}.hooks[{hookIndex}]
Step 17: Call hook.validate() to get array of HookDefinitionError results
Step 18: For each error in results, check isWarning property and append to appropriate array
Step 19: Use error.localizedDescription for the message field, defaulting to empty string if nil
Step 20: After all validation, construct ValidationResult with isValid = errors.isEmpty
Step 21: Implement public func validateJSON(_ json: String) -> Result<Void, Error> method
Step 22: Wrap JSONSerialization.jsonObject call in do-catch block
Step 23: Return .success(()) if parsing succeeds, .failure(error) if it throws
Step 24: Add documentation comments for all public types and methods

story_description: Provide debugging and testing capabilities for hook development, enabling developers to trace hook execution, inspect intermediate values, and identify issues during hook development without leaving the Blaze environment.
task_description: Create HookDebugService actor that integrates with Claude Code debug mode (CLAUDE_DEBUG=1), parses debug output for hook execution traces, and provides real-time monitoring of hook executions during development sessions.
atom_description: Implement HookDebugService actor providing three core capabilities: enableDebugMode() to configure CLAUDE_DEBUG=1 environment variable for subsequent CLI sessions, parseDebugOutput() to extract structured HookExecutionTrace records from debug log output, and startMonitoring() to provide real-time AsyncStream of hook execution events by watching debug logs during active sessions.
problem_statement: Hook development currently requires manual inspection of Claude Code debug logs to understand hook execution behavior. Developers must set CLAUDE_DEBUG=1 manually, locate the appropriate log files, and parse unstructured text output to trace hook execution. This workflow is error-prone and disconnects debugging from the visual builder context. Blaze needs a structured debug integration service that automates environment configuration, parses debug output into structured traces, and streams execution events in real-time for display in the hook builder UI.
